title: How the Panama Canal Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how the Panama Canal works and how it came to be. They cover Vasco Nunez de Balboa spotting the isthmus, early attempts by the Scottish and the French (including Ferdinand de Lesseps' sea-level plan that failed with heavy loss of life from disease and accidents), and the French company's collapse. They describe the US takeover in 1902 after Panama's independence from Colombia, the Chagres River dam creating Gatun Lake, the lock system, the mosquito and yellow fever control efforts led by William Gorgas, and the three-division construction under George Washington Goethals. They walk through the transit route and water use, then discuss the 1977 Carter treaty returning the canal to Panama on December 31, 1999, tolls, Panamax ship size, traffic, and the ongoing third-lane expansion. The episode closes with a listener mail about SEC oversight of oil reserve audits.
topics: SEC audit oil reserves listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and Panama earworm
segments.summary: The hosts open with chatter about the song Panama and a joke about misheard lyrics, then tease that the French did not finish the canal.

segments.title: Balboa and the isthmus
segments.summary: Balboa sees both the Pacific and Atlantic from a peak in Darien, realizing the narrow isthmus could be a shortcut. Trade with Asia and the long route around South America are described.

segments.title: Geography and early attempts
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difficulty of the terrain, including dense jungle, mountains and the Continental Divide, and early failed outposts by the Scots, Spanish and French.

segments.title: French sea-level canal and its failure
segments.summary: The French, inspired by steam technology, attempted a sea-level canal under Ferdinand de Lesseps. Disease, accidents and about twenty thousand deaths led to bankruptcy, and Eiffel's later lock proposal came too late. About eleven miles were dug.

segments.title: US takeover and Panama's independence
segments.summary: The US bought the French assets around 1902 and Congress backed Panamanian independence from Colombia. A treaty made the canal zone American soil, with Panama receiving about ten million dollars.

segments.title: Lock design, Gatun Lake and the Chagres River
segments.summary: Chief engineer John Frank Stevens chose a lock system. The Chagres River was dammed to form Gatun Lake, which carries ships over the mountains.

segments.title: Mosquito control, construction and transit route
segments.summary: Ronald Ross's mosquito findings led William Gorgas to sanitation work that controlled yellow fever. Goethals led three divisions, using steam shovels and dynamite. The hosts describe the transit route and water use.

segments.title: Carter treaty, tolls and expansion
segments.summary: The canal was returned to Panama on December 31, 1999 under a treaty negotiated by Jimmy Carter. Traffic, Panamax size limits, tolls by weight and cargo value, and the third-lane expansion are discussed, along with Richard Halliburton's swim.

segments.title: Listener mail on SEC oil reserve audits
segments.summary: A listener named Henry corrects an earlier episode's point about SEC audits of oil reserves, explaining that audit firms perform the audits under SEC and PCAOB guidelines.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give contact information for the show.
